newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Bombay paralysed by power failure.
newsitem.headline: India's Bombay paralysed by power failure.

text.p: A widespread power failure plunged many areas of India's commercial capital Bombay into darkness late on Friday, city officials said.
"Bombay, Thane and two other adjoining districts of Maharashtra are totally in the dark," an official at the state police headquarters told Reuters.
People making their way home from work were stranded as trains ground to a halt all over the state after the power was suddenly cut off, railway officials said.
"It's a grid failure. Trains all over Maharashtra have stopped in their tracks," a spokesman for the Central Railway suburban network told Reuters.
A spokesman for BSES Ltd., which supplies the bulk of Bombay's power, said the failure occurred after two major power stations near Bombay tripped.
But supply had not been affected in most of the city's northwestern suburbs, which is supplied by a third power station, he said.
Banks, brokerages and the offices of major newspapers, busy analysing the country's budget for 1997/98 (April-March) delivered a few hours earlier, had to stop work.
"We are in darkness but we see light in the stockmarkets," said at a dealer at a foreign brokerage, referring to the provisions of the budget, widely seen as market-friendly.
Officials of the state-run electricity board could not immediately be contacted for comment.

Power failures are quite common in India because the country's crumbling infrastructure is unable to satisfy the demand for energy, which has multiplied many times since free market reforms began to transform the economy in 1991.
Late in January, the nation's seniormost civil servant in the power ministry warned of the prospect of energy riots as India's power shortage began to assume alarming proportions.
In the capital New Delhi, blackouts are frequent, and across the country peak shortage is at an average 18 percent. High transmission and distribution losses also contribute to the shortage.
Power Minister S Venugopalachari has estimated that power shortages cost industry $2.7 billion annually, equivalent to 1.5 percent of the gross domestic product.
To offset the shortfall, he recently said, India needed around 100,000 MW of additional capacity involving an investment of four trillion rupees ($112 billion) over the next ten years.
